metadata.title: Lessons from PISA 2012 for the United States (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This chapter reports item-level solution rates for PISA 2012 mathematics items administered in the United States, comparing the United States to the OECD average and to five reference countries/economies. The analysis is conducted at the item level using solution rates (percent correct) and transformed logits to identify “conspicuous items” (unexpectedly large/small differences). The excerpt does not specify whether complex survey sampling weights or replicate weights were applied when computing solution rates, nor does it name any weight variables from the PISA database. For analysts using the underlying PISA microdata, the standard approach is to apply the PISA sampling weights (and replicate weights if available) to account for the complex two-stage sampling design; however, this chapter’s presentation focuses on descriptive item statistics and does not document a weight-aware estimation procedure.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable here because the chapter analyzes item-level solution rates (percentage of students answering each mathematics item correctly) and compares them across countries using logits derived from these solution rates, rather than estimating PV-based achievement scores. Missing-data handling is not reported because the excerpt does not describe any student-level analytic dataset construction or imputation/deletion rules; it instead summarizes publicly reported item solution rates and identifies conspicuous items based on differences relative to OECD/reference-country averages.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The chapter restricts attention to the 84 PISA 2012 mathematics items that were administered in the United States (paper-and-pencil assessment). It excludes two clusters of items that were used only in “easier” test booklets, which the United States did not use. The analysis is based on item solution rates (percent correct) for these 84 items, and then selects conspicuous items using logit transformations and thresholds based on standard deviations of logit differences.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD chapter uses PISA 2012 mathematics item-level data for the United States, focusing on the 84 paper-and-pencil mathematics items administered in the U.S. It computes solution rates (percent correct) for each item and transforms them into logits to place item success on a linear metric, then identifies “conspicuous items” where the U.S. differs from the OECD average and from five reference countries (Canada, Germany, Korea, the Netherlands, Shanghai-China) by at least one standard deviation in logit differences. The chapter reports overall solution rates (43.78% for the U.S. vs 47.47% OECD average) and enumerates 33 conspicuous items (16 relatively strong, 17 relatively weak). It further groups these items into cognitive “patterns” based on shared content and process requirements (e.g., interpreting/employing vs formulating; content areas such as Space and shape). No machine-learning model is trained; the results are descriptive and framework-based, so causal claims about curriculum effects are not established.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse for ML-related fields because the chapter is an OECD descriptive analysis of PISA item solution rates and cognitive patterns, not an empirical machine-learning study with a predictive target, model training, or reported PV-based scaling. Consequently, there is no ML algorithm evaluation, no PV handling, and no documented missing-data strategy at the student-record level in the provided text.
